text: You may replace at most k characters of s with any uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring of a single repeated letter you can get.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. So within some window, I keep the most frequent letter and replace the rest. That costs window length minus the count of the most frequent letter. The window is feasible if that cost is at most k. For A, A, B, A, B, B, A with k equal to one, the answer is four. Uppercase only, so twenty-six letters?
Yes, A to Z, and n is up to ten to the fifth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would check every substring's cost — quadratic at best, too slow for ten to the fifth. This problem reminds me of a variable-length sliding window — grow always, shrink while invalid, track the max — where I just swap in a new validity rule. Grow the right pointer; while window length minus max freq is above k, shrink from the left. The most-frequent count automatically picks the best letter to keep, so one pass covers all twenty-six letters. That's linear.
Do you recompute max freq when you shrink?

No — and that's the famous subtlety. I let max freq only ever increase. A stale, too-large max freq just makes the window reluctant to shrink, so it slides at a fixed size. The window only stretches past that size when a real, larger count shows up in the current window, so the answer is never over-counted. That saves the twenty-six-letter recount on every shrink.

Here's the plan. One: an empty count map, max freq zero, left at zero. Two: for each right pointer, count its letter and raise max freq. Three: while window length minus max freq is above k, drop the left end; then update the max length. One thing worth flagging — max freq is never lowered on purpose, for the reason I just gave. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop over the right pointer: bump the letter's count and fold it into max freq in the same line, shrink while the replacements needed exceed k, then record the window length. The easy line to get wrong is the condition — it's window length minus max freq, greater than k; flip either side and it breaks. And since the window never shrinks below its best size, the while runs at most once per step, so it can be an if.

Let's trace A, A, B, B, B with k equal to one — expected four. The row that matters is index four: the count of B truly becomes three, lifting max freq to three and the feasible length to four — the answer grows only because a real larger majority appeared. Just before that, at index three, the window A, A, B, B needs two replacements, so it slides to A, B, B. The result is four. That matches. Corner cases: k equal to zero degenerates to the longest run of one letter. And k at least n returns n.
How does this compare to a window that just forbids repeated characters?

Identical skeleton — only the shrink condition differs. No-repeats shrinks while a character's count is above one; here it shrinks while replacements are above k. A longest variable window is: grow always, shrink while invalid, track the max. Just swap what invalid means.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each of the two pointers crosses once, and max freq is never recomputed. Space is order twenty-six — fixed letter counts. Oh, one more thing — the cousins. For the longest run of ones when you may flip k zeros, just count zeros, no majority needed. And shortest-window variants flip the shrink to while valid.
Great. The length minus max freq validity, the insight that the majority covers all letters, and you nailed the stale max freq justification. Done.
